title: Home Is Where The Community Is
author: Michael Perrone
summary: Michael Perrone argues that the most practical frontier for building high-trust community is the family home, and that doing so is now countercultural enough to count as weird. He starts from the idea that modern homes lack the parlors, porches and dining rooms that once made hosting easy, then insists that hosting is a state of mind rather than a floor plan. He identifies the habit of treating home as a retreat from a draining day as the main obstacle, and says opening the door is exactly what restores energy. He welcomes the death of formal etiquette but offers a few new norms for guests and hosts, such as committing to invitations and being clear about expectations. He also defends a clean home as the baseline of family discipline and a sign that a household exists to build civilization rather than consume. His closing case is for the children, who gain a circle of invested adults and a picture of the good life beyond extracurriculars and screens.
points: Perrone reframes hospitality as a civic duty of the household: a home is a social asset that builds a corner of civilization, not only a private refuge.
The urge to treat home as an escape from the faceless crowd is the very thing that deepens loneliness, so welcoming people in is most valuable when you least feel like it.
Because old etiquette is dead, hosts and guests are free to set simple new norms, chiefly commit to an invitation, show up engaged, and state clearly what you want guests to bring or do.
A clean home is presented as the baseline of family discipline, since a messy default signals consumption and entropy rather than a purpose-driven household.
The deepest motive is for children, who gain adults invested in the family and evidence that the good life is more than atomizing activities and prestige TV.
quotes: Most of the people we encounter on a daily basis are not real, knowable people to us. They are an endless turnstile of faces to whom we owe no loyalty, no intimacy, no connection, nor kindness above what could be referred to as “basic human decency”.

The irony of this attitude is that the only true escape from the faceless horde is to get to know some of their faces, and make them more important to us than almost anything else. There’s nothing quite as energizing as genuine connection.

The bad news is there’s no longer any commonly accepted social etiquette around hosting, being a guest, and gathering for a meal, or a social event, etc. But this is also good news. You don’t have to worry about living up to old rules.
If you’re invited to something, commit one way or another. Do not waffle and then drop out at the last minute. Show up as your best self, engaged, present, and attentive to your host.
If you’re a host, be generous in what you provide, gracious in your manner of providing it, and clear about what you want people to do or bring.
Not keeping a clean home is forgetting what the home is for. Not keeping a clean home is entropy. It’s passive. It requires nothing of you.

We do it to offer them something that’s exceedingly rare today: a group of adults who are invested in our family. We do it to show them the good life transcends filling our family’s evenings and weekends with atomizing extracurriculars or prestige TV.
Loneliness and isolation are deadly to families. Only the weird will survive them. Only the weird will see their home as a social asset.
